blocks.text: Database concepts and the limits of the file system
An organised collection of related data stored so that it can be accessed, managed and updated easily and shared by many users and programs.

Software that creates, stores, retrieves, updates and protects a database and lets users and applications work with data without knowing how it is physically stored. Examples: MySQL, Oracle, PostgreSQL, SQLite.
Before DBMSs, programs kept data in separate **files** (a file system). Every application had its own files, which caused several problems that a DBMS removes.

blocks.caption: File system versus database (DBMS)
rows: The same data is repeated in many files
Controlled; data is stored once and shared
Copies can disagree after an update in one file
Much reduced, because there is a single copy
Each new query needs a new program
Flexible queries using a language such as SQL
Program depends on the file format; changing the format breaks it
Programs are largely independent of how data is stored
Rules are coded inside every program
Rules (keys, types, NOT NULL) are enforced centrally
Hard; users may overwrite each other
Managed for many users at once
User accounts and access rights on tables

blocks.text: A DBMS reduces redundancy and inconsistency, gives data independence and sharing, enforces integrity and security, and supports easy querying. A file system has none of these built in.
The relational data model: domain, attribute, tuple and relation
In the **relational model** data is organised in two-dimensional tables called **relations**. The model was proposed by E. F. Codd. Each table has a name, columns with names, and rows.

blocks.caption: Relational terms and their everyday names
rows: A set of tuples with the same attributes
One entry in the relation, such as one student
A named property, such as Name or City
The pool of permitted values for an attribute (for example Class in {XI, XII}; Marks 0 to 100)
Count of attributes in the relation
Count of tuples in the relation

blocks.text: Sample relation STUDENT used in this lesson (degree 4, cardinality 5):

Properties of a relation: each attribute has a unique name; every cell holds a single (atomic) value; the order of tuples and of attributes does not matter; and **no two tuples are identical**, since a relation is a set.
Do not mix up degree and cardinality: degree = columns, cardinality = rows. Adding a new row changes the cardinality only; adding a column changes the degree only.
Keys: candidate, primary, alternate and foreign
A **key** is an attribute or set of attributes used to identify tuples. Suppose EMP(EmpID, Aadhaar, Email, Name, Dept) where EmpID, Aadhaar and Email are each unique for every employee.
A minimal set of attributes whose values uniquely identify every tuple of the relation. A relation may have several candidate keys. In EMP the candidate keys are EmpID, Aadhaar and Email.
The one candidate key chosen by the designer to identify tuples. It must be unique and **must not be NULL**. A relation has exactly one primary key. Here EmpID may be chosen.
A candidate key that was not chosen as the primary key. If EmpID is the primary key, Aadhaar and Email are the alternate keys.

An attribute (or set) of one relation that refers to the primary key of another relation (or the same one). It creates a link between tables and supports **referential integrity**: a foreign key value must either match an existing primary key value in the referenced table, or be NULL.

Example: DEPT(DeptNo, DName) has primary key DeptNo. If EMP has a column DeptNo that refers to DEPT, then EMP.DeptNo is a foreign key. EMP is the referencing (child) table and DEPT is the referenced (parent) table. In the child table the foreign key may repeat (many employees in one department) and may be NULL.

blocks.caption: Key summary
rows: Treated as potential identifiers; the one chosen as primary cannot be NULL
Depends on rules; they are not chosen as primary

blocks.problem: A relation LIBRARY(BookNo, ISBN, Title, ShelfNo) has BookNo and ISBN unique for every book, while Title and ShelfNo can repeat. Find the candidate keys, a suitable primary key and the alternate key.
blocks.solution:
A candidate key must identify each row uniquely and be minimal. BookNo is unique, so it qualifies. ISBN is unique, so it qualifies. Title and ShelfNo repeat, so neither is a key on its own.

Candidate keys: BookNo and ISBN. Choosing one as the primary key leaves the other as the alternate key; for example BookNo as primary and ISBN as alternate.
blocks.answer: Candidate keys: BookNo, ISBN. Primary key: BookNo (or ISBN). Alternate key: the other one.

blocks.text: A foreign key is not unique in the child table, and it is **not** the same as the primary key of that table. A primary key can never be NULL, but a foreign key can.
Relational algebra: selection and projection
**Relational algebra** is a set of operations that take one or two relations as input and produce a new relation as output. The two unary (one-relation) operations are selection and projection.

Picks the **tuples (rows)** that satisfy a condition. Notation: $\sigma_{condition}(R)$. The result has the same attributes as R (the same degree) and only the rows that pass the condition (cardinality is the same or smaller).

Picks the stated **attributes (columns)**. Notation: $\pi_{A_1, A_2}(R)$. The degree of the result is the number of attributes listed, and **duplicate tuples in the result are removed**, so the cardinality can shrink.

blocks.problem: For the STUDENT relation above, evaluate $\sigma_{Class='XII' \wedge City='Delhi'}(STUDENT)$, $\pi_{City}(STUDENT)$ and $\pi_{Name}(\sigma_{Class='XII'}(STUDENT))$.
blocks.solution:
First expression: pick tuples with Class XII and City Delhi. Only Meena (3, Meena, XII, Delhi) satisfies both, so the result has 1 tuple and 4 attributes.

Second expression: take only City: Pune, Delhi, Delhi, Pune, Goa. Duplicates are removed, leaving Pune, Delhi, Goa: 3 tuples, 1 attribute.

Third expression: select Class XII first (Asha, Meena, Sia), then project Name: 3 tuples, 1 attribute.
blocks.answer: Cardinalities and degrees: (1 tuple, degree 4), (3 tuples, degree 1) with values Pune, Delhi, Goa, and (3 tuples, degree 1) with Asha, Meena, Sia.

blocks.text: Selection chooses rows (horizontal cut) and projection chooses columns (vertical cut). A projection result never contains two identical tuples.
Union, set difference and Cartesian product
These are binary operations on two relations R and S.

blocks.caption: Binary operations
rows: All tuples that are in R, in S or in both; duplicates are removed
R and S must be **union-compatible**: same degree and corresponding attributes with the same domains
Tuples that are in R but **not** in S
Union-compatible; $R - S \neq S - R$ in general
Every tuple of R joined with every tuple of S
No compatibility needed. Degree = degree(R) + degree(S); cardinality = card(R) x card(S)

blocks.text: For union-compatible relations with $m$ tuples in R, $n$ tuples in S and $c$ tuples common to both: the union has $m + n - c$ tuples; $R - S$ has $m - c$ tuples; $S - R$ has $n - c$ tuples.

blocks.problem: Relation R has degree 3 and 4 tuples. Relation S has degree 2 and 5 tuples. Find the degree and cardinality of $R \times S$. Then, for two union-compatible relations A (6 tuples) and B (4 tuples) with 3 tuples in common, find the sizes of $A \cup B$, $A - B$ and $B - A$.
blocks.solution:
Cartesian product: degree 3 + 2 = 5 attributes; cardinality 4 x 5 = 20 tuples.

Union: 6 + 4 - 3 = 7 tuples (the 3 common tuples are counted once).

$A - B$: 6 - 3 = 3 tuples. $B - A$: 4 - 3 = 1 tuple. Notice $A - B$ and $B - A$ are different.
blocks.answer: R x S has degree 5 and cardinality 20; union 7 tuples; A - B 3 tuples; B - A 1 tuple.

blocks.text: Because attribute names may clash in a Cartesian product, they are qualified with the relation name (for example STUDENT.Roll and MARKS.Roll). A selection on a Cartesian product, such as $\sigma_{STUDENT.Roll = MARKS.Roll}(STUDENT \times MARKS)$, gives only the meaningful pairs and is how a join is built from basic operations.
Union and difference need union-compatible relations; Cartesian product does not. Product: degrees add, cardinalities multiply. Selection = rows, projection = columns.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a disadvantage of keeping data in separate files for each application?
options: Data can be accessed without writing any program
The same data is repeated in many files, causing redundancy and inconsistency
Data is automatically protected by user accounts
questions.explanation: A file system keeps a separate file for each application, so the same fact (such as a student address) may be stored many times. When one copy is updated and another is not, the data becomes inconsistent. A DBMS stores data once and shares it.

optionRationale.3: That is a DBMS feature, not a file system feature.
optionRationale.4: In a file system each program has to implement its own rules.
optionRationale.1: This is false for files; each new kind of access usually needs a program.

questions.objective: Identify problems of the file system

questions.stem: A relation has 5 attributes and 4 tuples. What are its degree and cardinality?
questions.explanation: Degree is the number of attributes (columns), which is 5. Cardinality is the number of tuples (rows), which is 4. The two terms are not interchangeable. Checking the other options: Option 1: Degree counts the attributes (columns) and cardinality counts the tuples (rows); the values are swapped. Option 3: The product of the numbers is not the degree or the cardinality. Option 4: The two counts are not added together.

optionRationale.1: Degree counts the attributes (columns) and cardinality counts the tuples (rows); the values are swapped.
optionRationale.3: The product of the numbers is not the degree or the cardinality.
optionRationale.4: The two counts are not added together.

questions.objective: Define degree and cardinality

questions.stem: Which statement about a primary key is correct?
options: A relation can have several primary keys
It must be unique for every tuple and cannot contain NULL
It must be the first column of the table
questions.explanation: A primary key is the candidate key chosen to identify tuples. It must have a unique, non-NULL value in every tuple, and each relation has exactly one primary key. Checking the other options: Option 1: NULL is not allowed in a primary key. Option 2: A relation has exactly one primary key, though it may have several candidate keys. Option 4: The position of a column does not decide whether it is a key.

optionRationale.1: NULL is not allowed in a primary key.
optionRationale.2: A relation has exactly one primary key, though it may have several candidate keys.
optionRationale.4: The position of a column does not decide whether it is a key.

questions.objective: State properties of a primary key

questions.stem: In relational algebra, which operator is used to choose particular columns of a relation?
questions.explanation: Projection picks the listed attributes (columns) and removes duplicate tuples. Selection works on rows, while union and Cartesian product take two relations. Checking the other options: Option 1: Selection chooses rows that satisfy a condition. Option 2: Union combines the tuples of two relations. Option 3: Cartesian product pairs every tuple of one relation with every tuple of another.

optionRationale.1: Selection chooses rows that satisfy a condition.
optionRationale.2: Union combines the tuples of two relations.
optionRationale.3: Cartesian product pairs every tuple of one relation with every tuple of another.

questions.objective: Identify the projection operator

questions.stem: A column in table ORDERS holds customer numbers that must match the primary key of table CUSTOMER. What is this column called?
questions.explanation: An attribute that refers to the primary key of another relation is a foreign key. It links the child table ORDERS to the parent table CUSTOMER and supports referential integrity. Checking the other options: Option 1: A candidate key identifies tuples in its own table. Option 2: An alternate key is a candidate key not chosen as primary key, not a link to another table. Option 4: This is not a key in the relational model.

optionRationale.2: An alternate key is a candidate key not chosen as primary key, not a link to another table.
optionRationale.4: This is not a key in the relational model.
optionRationale.1: A candidate key identifies tuples in its own table.

questions.objective: Recognise a foreign key

questions.stem: Table EMP(EmpID, Aadhaar, Email, Name, Dept) has EmpID, Aadhaar and Email each unique for every employee, with EmpID chosen as the primary key. How many alternate keys does EMP have?
questions.explanation: The candidate keys are EmpID, Aadhaar and Email, a total of three. The primary key takes one of them (EmpID); the remaining two, Aadhaar and Email, are the alternate keys. Checking the other options: Option 1: Three candidate keys exist; one is the primary key, so two remain, not one. Option 2: The primary key itself is not an alternate key. Option 3: Candidate keys that are not chosen as primary key are alternate keys, so there are some.

optionRationale.1: Three candidate keys exist; one is the primary key, so two remain, not one.
optionRationale.2: The primary key itself is not an alternate key.
optionRationale.3: Candidate keys that are not chosen as primary key are alternate keys, so there are some.

questions.objective: Count alternate keys from candidate keys

questions.stem: The relation STUDENT(Roll, Name, Class, City) has these tuples: (1, Asha, XII, Pune), (2, Ravi, XI, Delhi), (3, Meena, XII, Delhi), (4, Karan, XI, Pune), (5, Sia, XII, Goa). How many tuples does the selection of Class = XII and City = Pune give?
questions.explanation: Check each tuple for both conditions together. Asha (XII, Pune) satisfies both. Meena and Sia are in XII but not Pune. Ravi and Karan are not in XII. So exactly 1 tuple qualifies. Checking the other options: Option 1: Three students are in class XII but only Asha is also in Pune. Option 3: Three tuples have Class XII, but the City condition must hold as well. Option 4: Asha satisfies both conditions.

optionRationale.1: Three students are in class XII but only Asha is also in Pune.
optionRationale.3: Three tuples have Class XII, but the City condition must hold as well.

questions.objective: Evaluate a selection with two conditions

questions.stem: For the same STUDENT relation of five tuples, the projection on City gives how many tuples, when the cities in order are Pune, Delhi, Delhi, Pune, Goa?
questions.explanation: Projecting on City produces Pune, Delhi, Delhi, Pune, Goa before duplicate elimination. A relation is a set, so duplicates are removed, leaving the three distinct tuples Pune, Delhi and Goa. Checking the other options: Option 1: Projection removes duplicate tuples from its result, so the repeated cities are not counted twice. Option 2: There are three different cities, not two. Option 4: More than one distinct city appears.

optionRationale.1: Projection removes duplicate tuples from its result, so the repeated cities are not counted twice.
optionRationale.2: There are three different cities, not two.
optionRationale.4: More than one distinct city appears.

questions.objective: Show that projection removes duplicates

questions.stem: Relation R has degree 3 and cardinality 4. Relation S has degree 2 and cardinality 5. What are the degree and cardinality of $R \times S$?
questions.explanation: In a Cartesian product each of the 4 tuples of R is paired with each of the 5 tuples of S, giving 4 x 5 = 20 tuples. Each result tuple has all attributes of both relations, so the degree is 3 + 2 = 5.

optionRationale.2: Degrees are added but cardinalities are multiplied; the degree is not a product and the cardinality is not a sum.
optionRationale.3: The cardinalities are multiplied, not added.
optionRationale.4: The degrees are added (3 + 2), not multiplied.

questions.objective: Compute degree and cardinality of a product

questions.stem: Match each relational algebra operation in List-I with its effect in List-II.
questions.explanation: Selection picks rows that satisfy a condition (II). Projection picks columns (IV). Union gives tuples that occur in either relation (I). Set difference gives tuples in the first relation that are absent from the second (III).

optionRationale.1: Selection does not combine two relations, and projection does not pair tuples.
optionRationale.3: Union returns tuples from either relation; difference removes tuples of S from R.
optionRationale.4: Selection picks rows, while projection picks columns.

questions.objective: Match operations with their effects

right: I. Tuples present in R or in S or in both
II. Rows that satisfy a condition
III. Tuples present in R but not in S

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements about keys.
A. A foreign key value in the child table may be NULL.
B. A relation may have more than one candidate key.
C. A primary key may contain duplicate values if the rows differ in other columns.
D. An alternate key is a candidate key that is not chosen as the primary key.
Which statements are correct?
questions.explanation: A is true: a foreign key can be NULL when there is no related parent row. B is true. D is the definition of an alternate key. C is false because primary key values must be unique and non-NULL regardless of other columns.

optionRationale.1: C is false and B and D are true, so this option leaves out correct statements.
optionRationale.2: C is false: primary key values must be unique.
optionRationale.4: C is false, so not all four statements are correct.

questions.objective: Judge statements about keys

questions.stem:
Assertion (A): A foreign key column can contain repeated values in the child table.
Reason (R): Many tuples of the child table can refer to the same tuple of the parent table.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: For example many students (child rows) can have the same ClassCode (foreign key) pointing to one row of the CLASS table. This many-to-one reference is exactly why repeated foreign key values are allowed, so the reason explains the assertion.

optionRationale.2: R is the direct explanation for the repetition, not just a related fact.
optionRationale.3: R is true: many child rows may reference one parent row.
optionRationale.4: A is true: foreign keys may repeat.

questions.objective: Explain repeated foreign key values

questions.stem: Union-compatible relations A and B have 6 and 4 tuples respectively, and 3 tuples appear in both. What are the cardinalities of $A \cup B$, $A - B$ and $B - A$ in this order?
questions.explanation: The union counts each distinct tuple once: 6 + 4 - 3 = 7. A - B removes from A the 3 tuples that also occur in B, leaving 3. B - A removes the 3 common tuples from B, leaving 1. So the sizes are 7, 3 and 1.

optionRationale.1: The 3 common tuples must be counted once in the union, so the union has 7 tuples, not 10.
optionRationale.2: B - A removes the 3 common tuples from the 4 in B, leaving 1.
optionRationale.4: The two difference results are interchanged: A - B has 6 - 3 = 3 and B - A has 4 - 3 = 1.

questions.objective: Apply set sizes of union and difference

questions.stem: Relation STUDENT(Roll, Name, Class, City) has tuples (1, Asha, XII, Pune), (2, Ravi, XI, Delhi), (3, Meena, XII, Delhi), (4, Karan, XI, Pune), (5, Sia, XII, Goa). What does $\pi_{Class, City}(\sigma_{City \neq 'Goa'}(STUDENT))$ return?
questions.explanation: The selection removes Sia, who lives in Goa, leaving four tuples. Projecting Class and City gives (XII, Pune), (XI, Delhi), (XII, Delhi) and (XI, Pune). These four combinations are all different, so no duplicate is removed and the cardinality stays 4.

optionRationale.2: The selection first removes the Goa tuple, so (XII, Goa) cannot appear.
optionRationale.3: Karan (XI, Pune) is not in Goa and is therefore kept, giving four tuples.
optionRationale.4: The projection keeps both Class and City, so the City values remain.

questions.objective: Combine selection and projection

questions.stem: R(id, p) has tuples (1, a), (2, b), (3, c). S(id, q) has tuples (1, x), (3, y), (3, z), (4, w). How many tuples does $\sigma_{R.id = S.id}(R \times S)$ contain, and what is the degree of the result?
questions.explanation: The Cartesian product has 3 x 4 = 12 tuples of degree 2 + 2 = 4. The condition keeps only pairs with equal id: id 1 matches (1, x); id 3 matches both (3, y) and (3, z). That is 3 tuples, and the degree stays 4.

optionRationale.1: The selection removes the pairs whose id values differ, so not all 12 pairs remain.
optionRationale.2: The Cartesian product keeps both id columns, so the degree is 4.
optionRationale.3: The id 3 of R matches two tuples of S, so there are three matching pairs in all.

questions.objective: Use selection on a Cartesian product

questions.stem:
Assertion (A): $R - S$ and $S - R$ generally give different results.
Reason (R): Set difference returns the tuples of the first relation that do not occur in the second, so it depends on the order of the relations.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: If R has tuples that S lacks, those appear in R - S but not in S - R, which collects the tuples that S has and R lacks. The order matters because the difference is defined from the first relation, which is why the two results usually differ.

optionRationale.2: R is the precise reason for A, so it explains it.
optionRationale.3: R is true: the first relation fixes what is returned.
optionRationale.4: A is true: the two differences are generally unequal.

questions.objective: Explain why set difference is not commutative

questions.stem: Relation EMP has the values in the column Dept: Sales, HR, Sales, IT, HR; in the column Phone: 111, NULL, 333, 444, 555; and in the column Code: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. Which column can serve as a primary key?
questions.explanation: A primary key needs unique and non-NULL values. Dept repeats values. Phone is unique among the non-NULL entries but contains NULL. Code has five different non-NULL values, so only Code qualifies. Checking the other options: Option 1: Sales and HR appear more than once, so Dept is not unique. Option 3: Phone contains a NULL, which a primary key cannot have, even though the other values are different. Option 4: Code is unique and has no NULL, so one column does qualify.

optionRationale.1: Sales and HR appear more than once, so Dept is not unique.
optionRationale.3: Phone contains a NULL, which a primary key cannot have, even though the other values are different.
optionRationale.4: Code is unique and has no NULL, so one column does qualify.

questions.objective: Choose a primary key from sample data

questions.stem: Table DEPT has DeptNo 10, 20, 30 (primary key). Table EMP has the foreign key DeptNo referring to DEPT. Which operation will the DBMS reject because it violates referential integrity?
options: Inserting an employee whose DeptNo is 40
Inserting an employee whose DeptNo is 20
Inserting an employee whose DeptNo is NULL
Inserting a second employee with DeptNo 10
questions.explanation: Referential integrity requires every non-NULL foreign key value to match an existing primary key in the parent table. DeptNo 40 does not exist in DEPT, so inserting such an employee is rejected. NULL and repeated valid values are allowed.

optionRationale.2: Department 20 exists, so the reference is valid.
optionRationale.3: A foreign key may be NULL, which means no department is assigned.
optionRationale.4: Foreign key values may repeat in the child table.

questions.objective: Apply referential integrity

questions.stem: Relation P has degree 4 and 6 tuples; relation Q has degree 3 and 5 tuples. What is the degree of the result of $\pi_{A, B}(P \times Q)$ when A is from P and B is from Q, and how many tuples can it have at most?
questions.explanation: The product has 6 x 5 = 30 tuples of degree 4 + 3 = 7. Projecting two attributes gives degree 2. Projection removes duplicate tuples, so the result can have at most 30 tuples, and fewer if any pairs repeat.

optionRationale.2: Projection keeps only the two listed attributes, so the degree is 2.
optionRationale.3: The product has 6 x 5 = 30 tuples; adding gives the wrong count and duplicates can only reduce the number.
optionRationale.4: The degree is not a product, and projection reduces the attributes to two.

questions.objective: Reason about degree and cardinality after projection of a product

questions.stem: What is meant by the domain of an attribute?
options: The number of tuples in the relation
The primary key of the relation
The name of the table that contains the attribute
The set of all permissible values for that attribute
questions.explanation: The domain is the pool of values from which an attribute can take its entries, for example integers from 0 to 100 for Marks or the set {XI, XII} for Class. Checking the other options: Option 1: That is the cardinality. Option 2: A key identifies tuples; it is not the domain. Option 3: The table name is not the domain.

optionRationale.2: A key identifies tuples; it is not the domain.
optionRationale.3: The table name is not the domain.

questions.objective: Define domain
